_comment: What a stall has on its shelf, above the five consumables in loot.json.
game/equipment.py holds the arithmetic and none of the values, the way
game/loot.py, game/rooms.py and game/progression.py do.
A piece is a NAME and an ATTRIBUTE BLOCK. It is not a weapon and it is not
worn -- there are no slots, nothing is replaced, and nothing can be sold
back. Buying one adds its block to run.earned permanently, exactly as the
Boots in loot.json already do with move_speed. That is the whole mechanism,
and it is deliberately the mechanism that already existed.
*** stall.offers: 0 IN data/rooms.json IS THE ROLLBACK. ***
At zero no piece is ever rolled, the stall draws the five goods and nothing
above them, and this file goes unread. The narrower rollback is below:
every rarity_scale set to 1 and every attributes block emptied leaves a
shelf that still rolls and still charges and does nothing, the same shape
loot.json's 'boots.amount: 0' has.
NOTHING IN THIS FILE IS MEASURED. autoplay never enters a panel and never
spends, so no price and no attribute here moves any recorded bracket -- and
by the same token nothing in the suite can see whether a single piece is
worth buying. The prices are set against a measured INCOME (~24,500g over a
full run) and against nothing else. Treat every number as an opening bid,
and change them with hands on a keyboard rather than with tools/balance.py,
which is structurally incapable of having an opinion about them.
THIS RE-OPENS A DOCUMENTED DEAD END, and that is deliberate. 'A damage or
speed or max-HP upgrade in the shop' was refused for years because it
needed a per-Entity stat layer that every lookup went through. That layer
is game/attributes.py and it now exists; the Boots were the first good to
cross the line and these are the rest. What has NOT changed is the caution
underneath it, restated above: nothing measures whether any of it is worth
buying.
_floor_comment: price = base * rarity_scale * (1 + floor_step * (floor - 1)), never below 1.
The same depth curve loot.json puts on a kill and rooms.json puts on a
chest, reusing the shape rather than inventing a third idea of what deeper
is worth. At 0.15 the fortieth floor prices a piece at 6.85x the first,
which is roughly what the fortieth floor pays -- so a stall stays about as
affordable at the end of a run as it was at the start.
Its own number rather than a read of loot.json's, so the shelf can be
re-tuned without touching what a kill pays. rooms.json's treasure block
duplicates the same 0.15 for the same reason.
_rarity_comment: The rarity IDS AND WEIGHTS are loot.json's -- one idea of rarity across the
project, rolled through the existing LootTable.roll_rarity at 60/25/10/4/1.
What a rarity means to a PIECE OF GEAR is this block, and it is
A 16x gold pile is the intended one-in-a-hundred event: it is a number, it
is spent, and it is gone. A 16x attribute block is permanent and compounds
with everything bought after it, so the same curve there would make one
lucky stall the run. 6x at the top is about as far as a permanent block can
go and still be a good roll rather than the end of the difficulty curve.
The scale multiplies the price by exactly the same factor it multiplies the
block, so a legendary is not a better DEAL than a common -- it is a bigger
one. What a rarity buys is the chance to spend a lot at once, which matters
precisely because a stall shows three pieces and then never again.
Integers on purpose. A block has to replay exactly, and 2.5 * 25 is the
sort of arithmetic that does not; see Attributes.scaled.
Every key here is checked against loot.json's tiers in BOTH directions at
load. A rarity the pool cannot price, or a price for a rarity that does not
exist, fails loudly instead of sitting there costing nothing.
_pieces_comment: AT MOST TWO ATTRIBUTES PER PIECE, and it is checked at load rather than
left to taste. The panel gives the blurb about 150 pixels between
LEFT + BLURB_X and the rarity word right-aligned at TALLY_RIGHT, and a
third field runs straight through it at 384px. The same constraint
shop.py's blurb templates are kept short for, stated as a rule because a
piece is content and content gets added by somebody who is not looking at
the panel.
Units are the attribute's own, which are per-mille for the three chance
fields and the crit multiplier and hundredths-per-tick for regen -- see
game/attributes.py. So crit_chance 35 is 3.5%, crit_damage 60 is +6% on a
crit, move_speed 30 is +3%, and regen 4 is 0.04 hp/tick, which is a little
over two a second. The panel converts; nothing in the arithmetic does.
Twelve pieces against three shown, so a stall is a menu of three of twelve
and two stalls in one run rarely repeat. The pool is deliberately wide and
shallow: every one of the eight attributes appears on at least one piece,
so no attribute is reachable only through a shrine.
Prices are all within about 2x of each other on purpose. The rarity roll is
what makes one shelf expensive and another cheap, and a base spread as wide
as the rarity spread would make the two dials indistinguishable from the
player's side of the panel.
